title: LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN
description: Return all rows from one table plus matching rows from the other. Learn when and how to use LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN, including finding unmatched rows.

data.text: INNER JOIN only returns rows that match on both sides. But sometimes you need to see *all* rows from one table, even when there is no match — for example, a list of all products with optional sales information. That is where LEFT JOIN (and its mirror, RIGHT JOIN) come in.

LEFT JOIN returns every row from the **left** table (the first table in the FROM clause) and matching rows from the right table. When a left row has no match on the right, the right-side columns come back as NULL.

data.title: LEFT JOIN syntax

data.caption: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table (T1) plus matched rows from the right (T2); unmatched right rows produce NULLs
data.definition:
flowchart LR
  subgraph LEFT["T1 (Left table)"]
    A1[Row 1]
    A2[Row 2]
    A3[Row 3]
  end
  subgraph RIGHT["T2 (Right table)"]
    B1[Row A]
    B2[Row B]
  end
  subgraph RESULT["Result"]
    R1[1 + A]
    R2[2 + B]
    R3[3 + NULL]
  end
  LEFT --> RESULT
  RIGHT --> RESULT

data.text: We want every product, even those that have never been sold. Products with no sales will show NULL in the order_id column:

data.title: List all products and their first order
data.code:
SELECT p.product_name,
       o.order_id
FROM   production.products p
LEFT JOIN sales.order_items o
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;

data.title: Find unmatched rows with WHERE
data.text: Adding WHERE order_id IS NULL to that query returns only the products that have never been sold — a classic 'find the gaps' pattern. Remember: the WHERE runs AFTER the join, so it filters the combined result, not the left table alone.

data.title: Products with no sales
data.code:
SELECT p.product_name
FROM   production.products p
LEFT JOIN sales.order_items o
    ON o.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.product_name;

data.text: Chaining LEFT JOINs across multiple tables

data.title: Three-table LEFT JOIN
data.code:
SELECT p.product_name,
       o.order_id,
       ord.order_date
FROM   production.products p
LEFT JOIN sales.order_items i
    ON i.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN sales.orders ord
    ON ord.order_id = i.order_id
ORDER BY ord.order_date;

data.text: RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the **right** table and matching rows from the left. Functionally, it is just a LEFT JOIN with the table order reversed. Most developers prefer LEFT JOIN and never use RIGHT JOIN, because mixing them can confuse readers.

data.title: RIGHT JOIN — same result as LEFT JOIN with tables swapped
data.code:
-- These two queries return the same data:

-- LEFT JOIN version
SELECT p.product_name, o.order_id
FROM   production.products p
LEFT JOIN sales.order_items o ON o.product_id = p.product_id;

-- RIGHT JOIN version
SELECT p.product_name, o.order_id
FROM   sales.order_items o
RIGHT JOIN production.products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id;

data.title: ON vs WHERE with LEFT JOIN
data.text: With INNER JOIN, putting a condition in ON or WHERE makes no difference. With LEFT JOIN it does: a condition in ON filters rows *before* deciding what to NULL-fill, while a condition in WHERE filters *after* — which can silently turn your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
LEFT vs. RIGHT vs. FULL at a glance

data.title: Key takeaways
points: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table; unmatched right columns become NULL
RIGHT JOIN is the same thing with the tables swapped — LEFT JOIN alone is almost always clearer
Add WHERE col IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN to find unmatched (orphaned) rows
Condition placement matters: ON filters before matching, WHERE filters after
You can chain multiple LEFT JOINs, but each one must have its own ON clause
